analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing employees, consumers, and franchisees into pre-dispute binding arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a Senate committee vote or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have declared that fine-print clauses requiring people to give up their day in court before a dispute ever arises are not enforceable for employment, consumer, and franchise disputes, or for claims under civil rights and other protections for parties with unequal bargaining power. Instead, companies would have to resolve those disputes in court. Unions would keep their own separate arbitration system under collective bargaining agreements. The bill never advanced past a Senate Judiciary subcommittee hearing.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees, consumers, credit card holders, cell phone and cable customers, patients, and franchise owners who today must sign away their right to a judge or jury as a condition of getting a job, opening an account, or buying a service. They would regain the right to have disputes heard in court, where proceedings are public, rules of evidence apply, and class actions are available [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: No predispute arbitration agreement could force arbitration of an employment, consumer, or franchise dispute, or a dispute under statutes protecting civil rights or regulating contracts between parties of unequal bargaining power.
A court, not an arbitrator, would decide whether an arbitration agreement is valid and enforceable, under federal law.

The bill's findings state that entire industries have adopted these clauses, that people often must accept them as a condition of having a job, getting medical care, buying a car, or opening a bank account, and that they frequently do not realize they have given up their rights.
The bill exempts arbitration under collective bargaining agreements, leaving union-negotiated arbitration systems intact.

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that use arbitration clauses to resolve disputes with customers, employees, and franchisees — including banks, credit card issuers, employers, and franchisors — would face lawsuits in court instead of private arbitration, which the bill's findings describe as costing them less and being easier to win [S3]. Arbitration companies would lose a large block of business from corporate repeat players [S3]. Companies could still use arbitration if agreed to after a dispute arises.
analysis.who_pays_short: Arbitration firms and corporations using arbitration clauses

drawbacks.text: Businesses argue that court litigation is slower and more expensive than arbitration, and that ending mandatory arbitration would drive up the cost of resolving small consumer and employment disputes, costs that could be passed on to customers.

The bill is a one-way rule: it does not fix arbitration itself (for example by requiring transparency or limiting biased clauses), it simply removes court access from anyone who signed a predispute clause, leaving the private arbitration system untouched for disputes where a court first decides it applies.
By drawing a line at 'predispute' agreements, it leaves open disputes over arbitration clauses agreed to after a dispute arises, which some may see as an invitation to argue over timing.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people, the benefit is substantial: the right to have disputes decided by a judge or jury in a public court instead of a private forum chosen and paid for by the other side. The cost falls on corporations and arbitration companies, and businesses warn it could raise the price of resolving small disputes. The bill also protects union arbitration from unintended disruption. On balance the design is straightforward and targeted, though it addresses only the predispute form of the problem rather than arbitration's other flaws.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where a subcommittee held a hearing in December 2007, but the committee never approved it and the full Senate never voted before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Feingold, joined by Sen. Durbin, introduced the bill on July 12, 2007; the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary.
Seven Democratic senators cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution held a hearing on December 12, 2007, with a printed hearing record.
No further action was taken before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporations that require arbitration clauses and the arbitration industry keep their current system, because the bill died in committee without a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Arbitration firms and corporations using arbitration clauses

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business groups
against.role: National business lobby opposed to limiting arbitration clauses
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed the Arbitration Fairness Act and similar later versions, arguing it would flood courts with disputes and raise costs for consumers.

sides.party_line_note: All eight sponsors were Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors, and the bill never advanced far enough to produce a floor vote with recorded party breakdowns.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and the private arbitration system
industries.note: The bill would remove employment, consumer, and franchise disputes from private arbitration, eliminating a major revenue stream from corporate repeat players, which the bill's findings describe as influencing how arbitration systems are designed.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, telecom, and other consumer-facing corporations
industries.note: These companies would no longer be able to enforce predispute clauses requiring customers to arbitrate, exposing them to court and class-action litigation; the bill's findings say such clauses are used to strip statutory rights, ban class actions, and move disputes far from people's homes.
Employment disputes would fall outside predispute arbitration clauses, restoring employees' access to courts for claims such as discrimination and wage disputes.
Franchise disputes would no longer be subject to predispute arbitration agreements, giving franchisees access to courts against their franchisors.
